title: Mainaka rises from the sea
hookLine: halfway across the sea, a golden mountain rises and offers Hanuman rest; how to honor a gift and keep a vow
carry: sankalpa: Rama's work first, then rest

lines: THE FIRST TEST IS A GIFT.
cards: You're driving a long way, late, and a friend texts: you're passing my town, come in, I've made dinner, sleep here. It's a real kindness. But if you stop, you won't get where you're going in time.
That's the first test Hanuman meets over the ocean, and it isn't a monster. It's a gift. The sea has been watching him, and the sea feels it owes him something.

teach.b: In Valmiki's telling, the Ocean is a person who thinks and remembers, and it remembers a debt.
Long ago King Sagara, an ancestor of Rama's own line, had sons who dug out the bed of the sea; tradition says that's why the ocean is called sagara.
So the Ocean thinks: this monkey is on an errand for Rama, of the family that made me what I am. He shouldn't wear himself out.

It calls to a mountain hidden beneath its waves, Mainaka, to rise and give the traveler a place to rest. Mainaka lifts out of the water, golden peaks shining, and invites Hanuman to rest, eat fruit, and then go on.
Hanuman's first reaction is suspicion, and he pushes the mountain aside with his chest. Then Mainaka explains, and Hanuman answers with great courtesy: I'm grateful; your welcome is as good as done.
But time is pressing, and I've promised not to stop. He touches the mountain with his hand and flies on.
Tulsidas, retelling the scene centuries later in his Ramcharitmanas, gives Hanuman a line many families know by heart: Ram kaju kinhe binu mohi kahan bishram.

teach.h: UNTIL RAMA'S WORK IS DONE, WHERE IS REST?
teach.b: Until Rama's work is done, where is rest for me?
That's sankalpa: a vow made before God, which comes before comfort. Hindus make one at the start of a puja or a fast, saying what they'll do and why.

teach.h: HE TOUCHES THE MOUNTAIN AND GOES ON.
teach.b: And Hanuman shows how to keep it kindly. No lecture, no resting a little to be polite. He honors the gift with a touch, and keeps the vow.

how: In Sundara Kanda recitations, Mainaka is the first of the meetings over the sea, and Tulsidas's line 'until Rama's work is done, where is rest for me?' is one many devotees know by heart; many families also keep a Tuesday fast for Hanuman.

games.q: you're keeping a Tuesday fast for Hanuman, and a friend's mom kindly offers you fresh brownies. by today's story, what fits?
o: eat one; a vow should bend so no one's hurt.
thank her warmly, explain the fast, and keep it.
say you're not hungry and leave it at that.
games.why: Hanuman touched Mainaka in thanks and kept his vow. sankalpa comes before comfort, and the gift still gets honored.

practice: Make a small sankalpa, the way Hindus do at the start of a puja or a fast. Hold a little water in your right palm, or just rest your hands together, and say silently one thing you'll do today and why.
If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, offer it to someone it will help. Breathe in, grateful for every comfort on offer. Breathe out, keeping the vow.

wordCard.voice: Mainaka. The golden mountain under the sea who rises at the Ocean's request to offer Hanuman rest, and whom Hanuman thanks with a touch before flying on.

orig.note: Sanskrit maināka, the mountain in the sea.

carryVoice: Your line: sankalpa, Rama's work first, then rest. Mainaka has a reason of his own, too. That's day six hundred six.
